title: Hungry for right (Matthew 5:6)
hookLine: blessed are those who hunger and thirst for what is right

cards: Hungry. Not a little peckish at four o'clock. Really hungry: a long hike, a fast, a day when everything went wrong and nobody remembered to eat.
Or thirsty on a hot day, when water is the only thought left. The whole body leans toward one thing. Few things in a life get wanted like that: a person, a home, a cure, a child who comes back.
The fourth line of the sermon names one more, and you can't eat it.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled." Righteousness can sound like a stiff, churchy word, even a little smug.
But the Greek word, dikaiosune, is bigger and warmer. It means being right with God, and it also means justice: things set right between people. Greek uses one word for both.

So does Hebrew: tsedakah, which is also the word Jews use for giving to the poor. So Jesus's listeners could hear both: a heart right with God, and a world where the widow gets fed and the worker gets paid.
The prophet Amos put it like this: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream."
Christians have leaned one way or the other at different times, and some hold both together: personal holiness and public justice. Now notice the verbs. Not blessed are the righteous.

teach.h: BLESSED ARE THE HUNGRY FOR IT.
teach.b: Blessed are the hungry for it: people who don't have it yet, who ache for it the way you ache for water. Nobody has to be finished. The blessing is on the wanting.
And the promise: they shall be filled.
The Greek word for filled, chortazo, is the one Matthew uses again when the crowds in the wilderness eat the loaves and fish and are filled.
Not a taste. A full meal.

how: Christians pursue righteousness both in personal prayer and repentance and in works of justice and charity: food banks, advocacy for the poor, and giving, which Christians in different churches see as part of the same calling.

o: keeping every religious rule perfectly and strictly
being right with God, and things set right between people
feeling morally better than the people around you

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: like the crowds fed in the wilderness

s: the Greek word for righteousness can also mean justice
the beatitude blesses those who are already righteous
it blesses those who hunger and thirst for it.
filled is the same word Matthew uses when the crowds ate the loaves
Matthew 14:20: they did all eat, and were filled.

games.q: you hear this line and think: I'm nowhere near righteous. who does Jesus actually call blessed?
o: the ones who have achieved it.
the ones who hunger and thirst for it.
the ones who talk about it most.
games.why: "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness." wanting it, badly, is where the blessing starts.

practice: Let one thing come to mind that isn't right: something big, like hunger, a war, an injustice in the news, or something close, like a family rift, a friend treated unfairly, something you did.
Don't argue with it; just feel the hunger for it to be made right, and notice where you feel it in your body. If you pray, you can offer that hunger to God.

wordCard.voice: Righteousness. Dikaiosune in Greek: being right with God and things set right between people, one word for both.

orig.note: Greek: righteousness, justice. one word for being right with God and setting things right.

carryVoice: Your line: hunger for good. Right with God and right between people: one word, one hunger. Until tomorrow.
